# U.S. ethics and regulatory analysis

This is planning information, not legal advice. State law, recruitment location, funding, data systems, and the researcher’s business structure can change the answer.

## Bottom line

On the facts given, this is probably **human-subjects research**, but it is not necessarily **federally regulated** human-subjects research.

- It is a systematic investigation intended to produce generalizable knowledge, and the researcher obtains information from living people through interaction or a research measurement procedure. That fits “research” and “human subject” under **45 CFR 46.102(l)** and **46.102(e)** ([current Common Rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title45-vol1/xhtml/CFR-2025-title45-vol1-part46-subpartA.html); [OHRP decision charts](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/sites/default/files/human-subject-regulations-decision-charts-2018-requirements.pdf)).
- The Common Rule ordinarily applies only when the research is conducted or supported by a federal Common Rule agency or is otherwise federally regulated: **45 CFR 46.101(a)**. OHRP’s decision chart expressly says that human-subjects research not conducted or supported by HHS is not covered by HHS regulations, although institutions may voluntarily apply them ([45 CFR 46.101](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title45-vol1/xhtml/CFR-2025-title45-vol1-sec46-101.html); [OHRP chart](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/sites/default/files/human-subject-regulations-decision-charts-2018-requirements.pdf)).
- A privately funded, unaffiliated researcher taking photographs directly from volunteers, without using a federally funded institution or testing an FDA-regulated product, therefore may have **no federal legal obligation** to obtain IRB approval.
- Nevertheless, prospective independent ethics review is strongly advisable. Major journals expect an IRB or ethics-board determination and generally do not want authors deciding for themselves that review was unnecessary ([ICMJE](https://icmje.org/recommendations/browse/roles-and-responsibilities/protection-of-research-participants.html); [JAMA instructions](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors/); [JAAD policy](https://jaad.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/22676537028759-Patient-Consent)).

The practical recommendation is to obtain an independent IRB’s written determination—exempt, expedited approval, or not federally regulated—**before recruiting or photographing anyone**.

## 1. Which federal regimes could apply?

### Common Rule: 45 CFR Part 46

**Legal requirement**

The Common Rule applies when a Common Rule department or agency conducts, supports, or otherwise regulates the research, subject to its exemptions: **45 CFR 46.101(a)**. If HHS supports nonexempt research, the engaged institution generally needs a Federalwide Assurance and IRB approval under **45 CFR 46.103** ([OHRP regulations](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/regulations/45-cfr-46/index.html)).

Federal coverage could arise later if, for example:

- The project receives an NIH, NSF or other Common Rule agency award.
- A federally supported university becomes engaged.
- A federal agency contract or award incorporates human-subject protections.
- An institution applies the Common Rule to all research as institutional policy, even when federal funding is absent. OHRP confirms that institutions commonly do this ([OHRP training](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ohrp-hrpf-lesson-1-english.pdf)).

**Common practice**

Even when federal jurisdiction is absent, an independent IRB can voluntarily review the study using the Common Rule framework. The determination letter should distinguish “not subject to the Common Rule” from “exempt under the Common Rule”; they are not the same conclusion.

### FDA regulations: 21 CFR Parts 50 and 56

**Legal requirement**

FDA IRB and consent regulations apply to clinical investigations involving an FDA “test article” or intended to support an FDA research or marketing submission: **21 CFR 56.101–56.103**. “Test article” includes drugs, biologics, devices and other FDA-regulated products ([21 CFR 56.101](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/56.101); [21 CFR 56.102(c), (l)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/56.102)).

Taking photographs, giving no treatment, and evaluating natural colour change ordinarily does not involve a test article. On the stated facts, FDA regulation therefore appears **not applicable**. That would change if the project tested a diagnostic device or software for an FDA submission, evaluated a drug or treatment, or generated evidence intended for an FDA marketing application.

### State and local law

The Common Rule does not displace more protective state, local or tribal law: **45 CFR 46.101(f)** ([current regulation](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title45-vol1/pdf/CFR-2025-title45-vol1-sec46-101.pdf)).

Relevant laws can include state medical-research consent statutes, privacy laws, data-breach laws and professional-licensing rules. For example, California has a statutory research-subject consent framework and Experimental Subject’s Bill of Rights ([California Attorney General guidance](https://oag.ca.gov/research/consent)); Washington’s My Health My Data Act regulates certain consumer health data outside HIPAA ([Washington Attorney General](https://www.atg.wa.gov/protecting-washingtonians-personal-health-data-and-privacy)). The applicable state requirements are **not found without knowing where the researcher and participants are located**.

## 2. Exempt versus expedited review

### Exempt review

The study is not an obvious fit for an exemption.

- **Category 2, 45 CFR 46.104(d)(2):** limited to educational tests, surveys, interviews and observation of public behavior. Private close-up skin photography is not public-behavior observation and is not expressly among the listed procedures ([45 CFR 46.104](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.104)).
- **Category 3, 45 CFR 46.104(d)(3):** covers brief, harmless, painless and noninvasive benign behavioral interventions with adult agreement and information collected through responses, data entry or audiovisual recording. An IRB might consider brief posing and standardized photography a benign behavioral intervention, but another IRB could conclude that the study has no behavioral intervention at all. Repeated sessions extending across many months also complicate the “brief in duration” requirement; SACHRP described brief interventions as lasting minutes to hours ([regulatory text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.104); [SACHRP recommendation](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/sachrp-committee/recommendations/attachment-b-august-2-2017.html)).
- **Category 4, 45 CFR 46.104(d)(4):** applies to certain secondary research using existing information or specimens, not prospective photography created for the study.

If Category 3 applies and images are readily identifiable, exemption can still be possible through limited IRB review under **46.104(d)(3)(i)(C)** and the privacy determination in **46.111(a)(7)**.

The investigator should not self-declare the exemption. OHRP recommends recording the specific exemption category, and JAMA tells authors not to make independent exemption determinations ([OHRP exemption FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/faq/exempt-research-determination/index.html); [JAMA instructions](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors/)).

### Expedited review

Expedited review is the most straightforward regulatory classification if the board does not grant exemption.

The official expedited list expressly includes:

> “Collection of data from voice, video, digital, or image recordings made for research purposes.”

That is expedited category 6, provided the IRB determines that the study involves no more than minimal risk ([OHRP expedited categories](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/categories-of-research-expedited-review-procedure-1998/index.html?locale=us)). Minimal risk is defined in **45 CFR 46.102(j)** by comparison with ordinary daily life or routine examinations.

Under **45 CFR 46.110**, expedited review is conducted by the chair or designated experienced reviewer. It does not mean that the study is exempt, and an expedited reviewer may approve or require changes but may not disapprove the study without convened-board review ([45 CFR 46.110](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title45-vol1/xhtml/CFR-2025-title45-vol1-sec46-110.html)).

With sensible privacy controls, no treatment, no invasive procedure, competent adults and a modest photography burden, expedited category 6 is a credible outcome. The IRB makes the final determination.

## 3. Commercial independent IRBs

FDA specifically recognizes that investigators can seek review from a university, hospital, government body or independent IRB ([FDA IRB FAQ](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/institutional-review-boards-frequently-asked-questions)).

A commercial IRB normally:

1. Contracts with the investigator, sponsor or research organization.
2. Reviews the protocol, consent form, recruitment materials, privacy plan, investigator qualifications and conflicts.
3. Determines whether the project is non-human-subjects research, exempt, expedited or full-board.
4. Issues stipulations, approval or a determination letter.
5. Reviews amendments, reportable events and closure as applicable.

IRB registration with OHRP is not certification or proof of competence; OHRP expressly cautions against treating registration that way ([OHRP registration FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/faq/irb-registration-process/index.html)). Ask about relevant experience, accreditation, indemnification, state-law review, record retention and whether the IRB accepts a sole unaffiliated investigator. Public confirmation that every named board will accept this exact arrangement was **not found**.

### Named examples, fees and timelines

| Independent IRB | Publicly documented fees | Published turnaround |

A current general **2026** public fee schedule was **not found** ([2025 schedule](https://research.rutgers.edu/system/files/2025-04/advarra-standard-irb-fee-schedule.pdf)). | A published workflow allocates **1 business day** for initial processing, **1–2 business days** for member review, and **1–2 business days** for final documents, excluding time awaiting responses ([workflow](https://ora.research.ucla.edu/OHRPP/Documents/Researchers/Advarra_IRB_Submissions_Training.pdf)). |

For budgeting, the directly posted examples range from roughly **$1,200** for an exemption determination to **$2,100–$3,500** for initial expedited or full-board review, with larger commercial-board arrangements potentially exceeding **$6,000**. Amendments, extra consent forms, annual review, HIPAA review and closure may be separate charges.

## 4. Consent for the photography study

### If the Common Rule applies

Nonexempt research generally requires legally effective consent under **45 CFR 46.116** and documentation under **46.117**, unless an IRB approves a waiver or alteration. The consent must explain purpose, duration, procedures, foreseeable risks, benefits, confidentiality, contacts and voluntariness; signed consent is the default unless documentation is waived ([45 CFR 46.116](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.116); [45 CFR 46.117](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title45-vol1/xhtml/CFR-2024-title45-vol1-sec46-117.html)).

A waiver would be difficult to justify when participants can readily be asked for consent. The general waiver test includes minimal risk, impracticability without the waiver, protection of rights and welfare, and additional restrictions when identifiable information is used: **46.116(f)(3)**.

### If the Common Rule does not apply

Federal research-consent rules may not be legally mandatory, but written consent remains the ethical and publication norm.

The form should address:

- The body area and frequency of photography.
- Whether images include tattoos, scars, jewelry or other identifiers.
- Whether photographs remain linked to names or a re-identification key.
- The difference between research participation and medical diagnosis or care.
- The possibility of incidental findings and the referral process.
- Storage location, access controls, retention and destruction.
- Whether images or derived data will be shared with other researchers.
- Whether images may be used for software or machine-learning development.
- Withdrawal procedures and what happens to previously analyzed or deidentified data.
- Whether identifiable images may be published online, in print or in presentations.

As common practice, consent to participate and permission to publish identifiable images should be separate choices. Refusing public image publication should not automatically prevent participation when the research can be reported with aggregate results or nonidentifiable crops.

## 5. Privacy and HIPAA

### When HIPAA does not apply

HIPAA regulates covered entities and their business associates, not every person holding health-related information. Covered entities are health plans, clearinghouses and health care providers that conduct specified electronic transactions: **45 CFR 160.103** ([HHS covered-entity guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/index.html)).

An independent researcher who recruits volunteers directly, takes the photographs personally, and is not acting for a covered entity will ordinarily not become HIPAA-regulated merely because the images concern skin. HHS states that the Privacy Rule does not give it authority over other private businesses through HIPAA ([HHS FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/who-must-comply-with-hipaa-privacy-standards/index.html)).

### When HIPAA may apply

HIPAA may apply if:

- A dermatologist or clinic supplies patient lists, records or clinical photographs.
- Images are created or stored through a covered medical practice.
- The researcher is a business associate performing services for a covered entity.
- A covered university medical center provides PHI.

A covered entity generally needs a valid HIPAA authorization under **45 CFR 164.508**, or a documented IRB/Privacy Board waiver under **164.512(i)**, for research use or disclosure of PHI ([HIPAA research guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/research/index.html); [45 CFR 164.508](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.508)). Research consent and HIPAA authorization are legally distinct, although the authorization can sometimes be combined with the research consent under **164.508(b)(3)**.

### Are close-up skin images identifiable?

HIPAA Safe Harbor expressly treats full-face photographs and comparable images as identifiers and also removes unique identifying characteristics or codes: **45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)** ([HHS deidentification guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/de-identification/index.html)). A tightly cropped spot photograph is not automatically a “full-face photograph,” but it may remain identifiable through a tattoo, distinctive scar, anatomical context, embedded metadata or a linked participant code.

Under the Common Rule, coding does not necessarily make data nonidentifiable if the investigator can readily obtain the key: **45 CFR 46.102(e)**. Under HIPAA, deidentification requires either Safe Harbor or a documented expert determination that reidentification risk is very small: **164.514(b)**.

### Data safeguards

If HIPAA applies, the Security Rule requires a risk analysis and reasonable administrative, physical and technical safeguards under **45 CFR 164.308–164.312**; encryption is “addressable,” meaning it must be implemented when reasonable and appropriate or replaced with a documented equivalent safeguard ([HHS security guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/guidance/guidance-risk-analysis/index.html); [encryption FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/is-the-use-of-encryption-mandatory-in-the-security-rule/index.html)).

Whether or not HIPAA applies, common practice is to disable consumer-cloud photo synchronization, use coded filenames, remove unnecessary EXIF metadata, keep the identity key separately, encrypt devices and backups, restrict access, document retention and deletion, and maintain a breach-response plan.

Non-HIPAA consumer-health-data laws may still apply. The FTC Health Breach Notification Rule reaches certain vendors of personal health records and related non-HIPAA entities, but whether a small private study constitutes such a vendor is **not found without its business and technology model** ([FTC guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/complying-ftcs-health-breach-notification-rule-0)).

## 6. Adding a dermatologist

Adding a dermatologist does not by itself create federal jurisdiction.

It can change the analysis if the dermatologist:

- Recruits from a clinical practice.
- Reviews or supplies medical records.
- Takes photographs as part of the practice.
- Diagnoses the lesions or returns clinical findings.
- Acts as an employee or agent of a university or hospital.

A health care practice is a HIPAA covered entity only if it meets the covered-entity definition, but most electronically billing medical practices do. Research access to its identifiable records or photographs would generally require authorization or a waiver.

If the dermatologist’s institution is involved, OHRP considers an institution engaged when its employees obtain research data through interaction or intervention, obtain identifiable private information, or obtain consent ([OHRP engagement guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/guidance-on-engagement-of-institutions/index.html)). The institution may therefore insist on its own IRB or a formal reliance agreement.

Common practice would also add:

- A documented process for confirming that an apparent benign lesion does not require clinical assessment.
- Clear separation between research measurements and medical advice.
- A plan for incidental concerning findings.
- Appropriate professional liability and state-scope-of-practice review.

Exact state licensing and malpractice requirements are **not found without the state and the dermatologist’s role**.

## 7. Adding a university

A university will almost certainly require submission to its human-research protection program under institutional policy, even if federal law would not have required review for the original private project. OHRP confirms that institutions commonly apply Common Rule procedures beyond federally supported research ([OHRP training](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ohrp-hrpf-lesson-1-english.pdf)).

If university personnel recruit, consent, photograph participants or receive identifiable data, the university is generally engaged. If HHS supports the study, the university needs an applicable FWA and IRB coverage under **45 CFR 46.103**.

Possible arrangements include:

- The university IRB becomes the reviewing IRB.
- The university formally relies on the existing commercial IRB.
- The commercial IRB relies on the university IRB.

External reliance must be documented, including allocation of regulatory responsibilities: **45 CFR 46.103(e)** ([OHRP reliance FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/faq/irb-registration-process/index.html)). For federally covered cooperative research involving multiple U.S. institutions, **45 CFR 46.114** generally requires a single reviewing IRB, subject to stated exceptions ([45 CFR 46.114](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title45-vol1/xhtml/CFR-2025-title45-vol1-sec46-114.html)).

A university can also extend its FWA to an unaffiliated collaborating investigator through an Individual Investigator Agreement when the regulatory conditions are met ([OHRP FWA FAQ](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/register-irbs-and-obtain-fwas/fwas/assurance-process-faq/index.html)).

The independent researcher cannot assume the university will accept a previously obtained commercial approval; approval and reliance should be settled before the university begins any study activity.

## 8. Adding skin biopsies

Research-only biopsies substantially change the risk and review route.

- A punch or shave biopsy is invasive and cannot qualify as a benign behavioral intervention under **46.104(d)(3)**.
- The expedited category for prospective biological-specimen collection is limited to specimens obtained by noninvasive means. A research-only skin biopsy does not fit that category ([OHRP expedited list](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/guidance/categories-of-research-expedited-review-procedure-1998/index.html?locale=us)).
- Because expedited review requires both minimal risk and a listed category under **46.110**, a research-only biopsy would commonly require convened-board review. Final classification belongs to the IRB.
- If a biopsy is clinically indicated and performed for care, and research uses leftover tissue, exemption under **46.104(d)(4)** or expedited category 5 may be possible depending on identifiability, consent, HIPAA and how the specimen was obtained.

The protocol would need qualified clinical personnel, sterile technique, wound care, management of bleeding, infection, scarring and allergic risks, adverse-event procedures, and state-law review of who may perform the biopsy. Exact state requirements are **not found without a jurisdiction**.

Consent should address tissue storage and future use. Where applicable, **45 CFR 46.116(c)(7)–(9)** calls for statements about possible commercial profit, return of clinically relevant results and possible whole-genome sequencing ([45 CFR 46.116](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.116)).

If tissue testing produces patient-specific results used for health assessment or diagnosis, the laboratory generally needs appropriate CLIA status. Research laboratories that do not report patient-specific results for diagnosis, treatment or health assessment are excepted under **42 CFR 493.3(b)(2)** ([42 CFR 493.3](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/493.3); [CMS guidance](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/legislation/clia/downloads/research-testing-and-clia.pdf)).

## 9. Publication requirements

Publication rules are not statutes, but they can be stricter than the legal minimum.

- **ICMJE:** investigators should obtain approval from an independent review body and be prepared to provide documentation. Identifiable photographs require written consent for publication, and the identifiable participant should be shown the material to be published ([ICMJE participant protection](https://icmje.org/recommendations/browse/roles-and-responsibilities/protection-of-research-participants.html)).
- **JAMA Network:** requires formal approval, waiver or a documented regulatory/institutional determination; authors should not decide exemption themselves. Identifiable photographs require signed publication consent, including where the participant can identify themselves ([JAMA instructions](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors/)).
- **JAAD:** states that studies involving patients or volunteers require ethics-committee approval and informed consent. Written consent is expected for use of patient data and images, including notice of online and other publication media ([JAAD consent policy](https://jaad.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/22676537028759-Patient-Consent)).
- **Nature Portfolio:** manuscripts must identify the approving ethics committee and reference number, or the committee granting exemption, and state that participant consent was obtained. Identifiable images need publication consent ([Nature research-ethics policy](https://www.nature.com/nature-portfolio/editorial-policies/ethics-and-biosecurity)).

Because no intervention is assigned, the project is ordinarily observational rather than a clinical trial. ICMJE encourages registration of observational studies but does not require it; compulsory ICMJE registration applies to prospectively assigned health interventions ([ICMJE registration FAQ](https://www.icmje.org/about-icmje/faqs/clinical-trials-registration/)). Voluntary preregistration is nevertheless useful.

A defensible publication file should contain:

- The dated protocol and analysis plan.
- Independent IRB determination or approval obtained before enrollment.
- Approved consent and image-publication forms.
- Recruitment materials.
- Data-security and retention plan.
- Amendment history.
- Documentation of consent for every published potentially identifiable image.
- A manuscript ethics statement naming the IRB, decision, date and reference number.
- An explanation of funding, conflicts, participant compensation and whether a dermatologist provided clinical oversight.
